title: Rendering React on the Server
summary: Do each rendering strategy with React itself: CSR with Vite, SSR and hydration, static prerendering, ISR through a CDN, and Server Components.
intro: The Where HTML Is Made lesson compared where a page's HTML can be made: in the browser, on a server for each request, at build time, or rebuilt now and then. This lesson does each of those with React itself, on a small Trailhead product page, so you can see the real HTML each one sends and the code that makes it. You'll start from the empty page a Vite build gives you, then stream HTML from a Node server, hydrate it in the browser and fix the mismatches that break hydration, prerender pages at build time, cache them on a CDN, and finish with Server Components and how to choose a framework that does all of this for you.

steps.title: What Vite builds: client-side rendering
steps.body:
Before you add a server, look at what you already have. A Vite React app is client-side rendered, CSR from the Where HTML Is Made lesson, and knowing exactly what it sends tells you what server rendering would add, and when you don't need it. ## The shell Run `npm run build` in the shop, and `dist/` holds an `index.html`, one JavaScript file, and one CSS file, as the first example shows. This is the whole `index.html`: ```html Trailhead
``` There's no product, price, or heading in it. `
` is empty, and the page only appears after the browser downloads 457 kB of JavaScript, runs it, and the app fetches its data. A search engine that doesn't run JavaScript, or a chat app making a link preview, sees a page called Trailhead with nothing on it. ## One file for every address The same file answers every address in the app. The second example asks for `/products/storm-shell-jacket` and gets the shell back, word for word. That only works because the server is set up to do it, with the SPA fallback from the Routing and App Structure lesson: any path that isn't a real file gets `index.html`. ## What it costs, and when it's enough The Where HTML Is Made lesson weighed this up. CSR is cheap to host, since the whole site is a folder of files, and quick to move around in once it's loaded. But a mid-range phone on a slow network takes a few seconds to download and run that 457 kB bundle, and only then does the app ask the API for the product, so LCP lands after both waits. The same page from a server would show the product in the first response. CSR fits when the people who matter are logged in and nobody needs to find the page in a search: dashboards, admin tools, account settings, the cart and checkout. It falls short when the first view has to be fast on slow phones, or when search and link previews matter, like a shop's product pages. Those are the pages the rest of this lesson renders on a server.

examples.title: Building the shop
examples.prompt: In the shop's folder. `build` runs `tsc -b` to check the types, then `vite build`.
examples.explanation: Vite read `index.html`, followed every `import` from `src/main.tsx`, and wrote three files. The JavaScript is 457 kB, about 141 kB once compressed with gzip, as the web course explained. That's React, React DOM, the router, TanStack Query, zod, Zustand, and the shop's own code, and the browser has to download and run all of it before a single product shows. The file names carry a hash of their contents, so they can be cached forever. `index.html` has no hash, since its name is how every visit starts.

examples.title: Every address gets the same shell
examples.prompt: With `npm run preview` running, ask for a product page, the way a search engine's crawler would.
examples.explanation: This is `dist/index.html`, byte for byte, even though the URL names a product. Vite's preview server applies the SPA fallback for you. The browser then loads the script, React Router reads `/products/storm-shell-jacket` from the address bar, and the product page fetches the Storm Shell Jacket from the API. A crawler that doesn't run JavaScript stops at this response, and all it learns is the title Trailhead. That's the gap server rendering fills.

steps.title: Streaming HTML with renderToPipeableStream
steps.body:
Server rendering means running your components on a server and sending the HTML they make, so the content is in the very first response. React does that with `react-dom/server`, which comes in the same `react-dom` package you already have. Streaming lets the fast parts of the page leave before the slow parts are ready. ## Rendering on the server `react-dom/server` has a few functions, and they differ in how they hand back the HTML: - `renderToString` returns all of it as one string. It's the oldest, and it can't wait for data: anything that would suspend just shows its fallback. - `renderToPipeableStream` writes the HTML to a Node **stream**, a way of sending data in pieces as they're ready instead of all at once. This is the one for a Node server. - `renderToReadableStream` does the same with the web's own streams, for servers that use them, like Deno, Bun, and Cloudflare Workers. ## The page The first example is the page, `src/App.tsx`. It renders the whole document, from `` down, which React 19 handles, so the server sends one complete page. The product is passed in as data. The reviews are passed in as a **promise**, the value a call like `fetch` returns, which settles later. `Reviews` reads it with `use(reviews)`. `use` is React's hook for reading a promise: if it hasn't settled yet, the component **suspends**, which means React stops rendering it for now and shows the nearest `Suspense` boundary's fallback instead. ## The stream The second example, `src/entry-server.tsx`, renders that page for one request. It awaits the product, which is fast, but not the reviews, which take a second. Then `renderToPipeableStream` starts rendering, and calls `onShellReady` as soon as everything outside a `Suspense` boundary is done: the **shell**. The server sends that part at once. ```diagram server-rendering-stream The shell leaves at once. The reviews follow a second later, in the same response. ``` In step 1 of the diagram, the shell arrives: the heading, the price, the button, and the fallback, Loading reviews…, in place of the list. The browser shows it right away, and starts downloading the JavaScript, which the shell asks for. In step 2, a second later, the reviews are ready, and React sends their HTML in the same response. In step 3, a tiny inline script that came with that chunk moves the reviews into place, where the fallback was. Each piece of the response looks like this, with line breaks added, React's helper script shortened, and the small comments it puts between pieces of text left out: ```html

Loading reviews…

  • Dry all day (5 of 5)
  • Packs small (4 of 5)
``` The comments `` and `` mark where the boundary starts and ends, and `B:0` names the spot. The later chunk arrives hidden as `S:0`, and `$RC("B:0","S:0")` swaps it in. All of this happens before React itself has loaded, so the reviews show up even on a slow phone. ## The other options `bootstrapModules` lists the scripts the page needs. React adds a `` in it would end the script early and let the rest run as HTML, the XSS from the Web Vulnerabilities and Secrets lesson. So `dataScript` in `src/dataScript.ts` escapes every `<` as `\u003c`, which JavaScript still reads as `<`. `onShellError` runs if the shell itself fails, and sends a 500, since nothing has been sent yet. `onError` logs errors from anywhere in the page. An error inside a `Suspense` boundary after the shell has gone doesn't break the page: React sends the fallback and lets the browser try that part again. The third example measures the stream with a small script, `watch-stream.mjs`, that prints when each chunk arrives: ```javascript // Prints each piece of a streamed response as it arrives. const start = Date.now(); const response = await fetch(process.argv[2]); const decoder = new TextDecoder(); for await (const chunk of response.body) { const text = decoder.decode(chunk); console.log(`${Date.now() - start} ms, ${chunk.length} bytes: ${text.slice(0, 60)}…`); } ```

examples.title: A page with a slow part
examples.prompt: `src/App.tsx` in a small Vite project, `trailhead-ssr`. `getReviews` in `src/data.ts` waits one second, standing in for a slow reviews service.
examples.explanation:
Everything outside `` is ready as soon as React has the product, so it's in the shell. `Reviews` calls `use(reviews)` on a promise that's still waiting, so it suspends, and `

Loading reviews…

`, the fallback, takes its place in the shell. When the promise settles, React renders `Reviews` with the list and streams it. `QuantityButton` is there to prove hydration later: on the server it renders as plain HTML with `Quantity: 1`, and the click only works once React has taken over in the browser. The `Updated` line formats its date with `timeZone: "UTC"`, a detail part 4 explains.

examples.title: Rendering one request
examples.prompt: `src/entry-server.tsx`, the server's side of the app. Vite builds it into `dist/server/entry-server.js`, which the Node server in part 3 imports.
examples.explanation: `render` gets a slug, a Node response, and the address of the client's bundle. A missing product gets a 404 before any rendering starts. `getReviews(slug)` without `await` starts the slow call and keeps the promise, so the shell doesn't wait for it. `onShellReady` sets the status and headers, then `pipe(res)` connects React's stream to the response, so every chunk goes out the moment React has it. Headers can't change after that, since they've already been sent. The `Cache-Control` header is for the CDN in part 5. `getReviews` is exported too, so the server can answer the browser's own request for reviews.

examples.title: Watching the chunks arrive
examples.prompt: With the server from part 3 running on port 8080, time the response.
examples.explanation: The response came in two pieces. The first, 980 bytes, arrived after 48 milliseconds: the shell, which is everything a visitor needs to start reading. The second arrived a full second later, when `getReviews` finished, and holds the hidden reviews and the script that swaps them in. Without streaming, the server would have waited the whole second before sending anything, and the visitor would have stared at a blank page. Your times will differ a little, but the gap of about a second won't.

steps.title: The server, the client entry, and hydration
steps.body:
The HTML from the previous part shows the product, but the Quantity button does nothing when clicked. No event handlers came with it, since functions can't travel in HTML. Hydration is the step that makes the page work, and it needs a server that sends the JavaScript and a client entry that takes over.

## Two builds

A server-rendered app is built twice from the same components. The **client build** makes the JavaScript for the browser, as a normal Vite build does. The **server build**, with `vite build --ssr`, makes a module for Node that exports `render`, with React and the other packages left as imports, since Node can load them from `node_modules`. The project's `package.json` has a script for each, plus one for part 5's prerendering:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build:client": "vite build --outDir dist/client",
    "build:server": "vite build --ssr src/entry-server.tsx --outDir dist/server",
    "build:prerender": "vite build --ssr src/entry-prerender.tsx --outDir dist/prerender",
    "build": "npm run build:client && npm run build:server && npm run build:prerender",
    "prerender": "node prerender.js",
    "start": "node server.js"
  }
}
```

The client bundle's name has a hash in it, like `entry-client-XwaCUWA8.js`, which changes with every change to the code. So `vite.config.ts` sets `build.manifest: true`, and Vite writes `dist/client/.vite/manifest.json`, a small file that maps `src/entry-client.tsx` to the hashed name. The server reads it to know what to put in `bootstrapModules`.

## The server

The first example is the whole server, `server.js`, using `node:http`, Node's built-in HTTP module. It does three jobs: it sends the built JavaScript from `dist/client/assets`, it answers the browser's request for reviews, and it renders product pages. In a real app, a framework or a small library like Express handles the first two, with care around file paths and content types. The rendering part is the same.

## Hydration

The browser shows the HTML as it streams in. Then the module script from `bootstrapModules` loads and runs `src/entry-client.tsx`, the second example. It calls `hydrateRoot` instead of `createRoot`. `createRoot` builds the DOM from nothing. `hydrateRoot` expects the DOM to be there already: React renders the same components in the browser and walks the existing HTML alongside its element tree, matching each element to the one already on the page. Where they match, React keeps the element and attaches its event handlers, so nothing is rebuilt and nothing flickers.

```diagram server-rendering-hydrate
The server's HTML and the browser's render meet in hydrateRoot. Matching nodes get their handlers.
```

In the diagram, the HTML on the left came from the server and the element tree on the right came from rendering in the browser. Hydration pairs them up, node by node, and the button gets its `onClick`. After that, the page is an ordinary React app: state changes render in the browser, and clicking Quantity counts up.

## The same data on both sides

For the trees to match, the browser has to render with exactly the data the server used. That's why the server put the product in `window.__PRODUCT__`, and why `hydrateRoot` gets `<App product={product} ... />` with that same object. If the client fetched the product again, it might get a newer price, and the page wouldn't match the HTML.

The reviews are different here: they streamed in as HTML, but their data didn't come along. So the client entry fetches them from `/api/reviews/storm-shell-jacket`, and the `Suspense` boundary waits for that promise before it hydrates the list. Until then, React leaves the server's HTML in place. That costs a second request for data the server already had. Frameworks avoid it by streaming the data too, alongside the HTML, which is a big part of what they do for you.

examples.title: A small Node server
examples.prompt: `server.js` in the project's root, run with `npm start` after `npm run build`.
examples.explanation: The `await` at the top of the file, which ES modules allow outside any function, reads the manifest once, when the server starts, and builds the bundle's address, like `/assets/entry-client-XwaCUWA8.js`. Asset files get `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, which the web course explained: their names change whenever their contents do, so a browser may keep them for a year. Each product URL goes to `render`, which streams the page into `res`. Everything else is a 404. The server listens on `127.0.0.1`, so only your own computer can reach it.

examples.title: Taking over the page in the browser
examples.prompt: `src/entry-client.tsx`, the client build's entry, which `build.rolldownOptions.input` in `vite.config.ts` points at.
examples.explanation: `declare global` tells TypeScript about the two values a page can carry on `window`. A server-rendered page carries only `__PRODUCT__`, so the reviews are fetched. A page prerendered in part 5 carries `__REVIEWS__` too, and `Promise.resolve` wraps them so `use` gets the promise it expects. Then `hydrateRoot(document, ...)` takes over the whole document, since `App` renders from `<html>` down. Opened in a browser, the page shows the product at once, the reviews a second later, and a click on the button changes it to Quantity: 2.

steps.title: When hydration doesn't match
steps.body:
Hydration only works if the browser renders exactly what the server did. When it doesn't, React can't trust the HTML, and the page flickers or loses what the server did for it. These bugs only show up with server rendering, so they're new even to people who know React well. ## What goes wrong React compares the HTML with its first render in the browser. If a piece of text or an attribute differs, that's a **hydration mismatch**. React 19 throws the server's HTML away for the part that differs, up to the nearest `Suspense` boundary or the whole page, and renders it again in the browser, as plain CSR would. The page still works, but visitors see a flash as it's replaced, the server's work for that part is wasted, and in development React reports an error. ## The usual causes The same component gives different output in two places when it depends on something that differs between them: - **The time.** `new Date()`, `Date.now()`, and anything that formats them. The server rendered at one moment and the browser a few seconds later, and they may be in different time zones too. - **Randomness.** `Math.random()`, or `crypto.randomUUID()` for an id. - **Checks for the browser.** `typeof window !== "undefined"`, `window.innerWidth`, `localStorage`, or `navigator.language` all differ, or don't exist, on the server. - **The visitor's settings.** `toLocaleDateString()` with no options uses the computer's own language and time zone, and the server's are almost never the visitor's. - **HTML the parser fixes.** A `
` inside a `

`, or a `` with no ``, gets rearranged by the browser when it reads the HTML, as the web course described, so the DOM no longer matches React's tree. - **Browser extensions** that add elements to the page before React loads. ## A real one The first example is the bug the shop's page had before its fix. The product's `updatedAt` is `2026-10-01T02:00:00Z`, two in the morning on October 1 in UTC. The server runs in UTC and wrote 10/1/2026. A visitor in Los Angeles is seven hours behind, where it's still September 30, so the browser wrote 9/30/2026. In development, React's error says what it saw, with `+` for what the browser rendered and `-` for what the server sent. A production build of React leaves its long messages out to keep the bundle small, so the same page, built with `npm run build`, reported only this, which the script tagged `[pageerror]`: ```text [pageerror] Minified React error #418; visit https://react.dev/errors/418?args[]=text&args[]= for the full message or use the non-minified dev environment for full errors and additional helpful warnings. ``` The link opens the full message on react.dev. When a code like 418 shows up in reports from real visitors, reproduce it with a development build to get the diff. ## The fixes - **Make both sides agree.** Format dates with an explicit time zone, as the fixed line now in `App.tsx` does, or format them once on the server and send the string as data. - **Render it after hydration.** For something that really is browser-only, like the visitor's local time or their screen size, render a neutral placeholder first and fill it in from an effect, which only runs in the browser, after hydration: ```tsx function LocalTime() { const [now, setNow] = useState(null); useEffect(() => setNow(new Date().toLocaleTimeString()), []); return

Local time: {now ?? "…"}

; } ``` - **Use `useId` for ids.** A label and its input need matching `id` and `htmlFor` values. A random one differs on each side. `useId()` gives a value based on the component's place in the tree, which is the same on the server and in the browser: ```tsx function QuantityField() { const id = useId(); return ( <> ); } ``` - **`suppressHydrationWarning`** on one element tells React that its text is allowed to differ, like a timestamp that's fine either way. It only covers that one element's own text and attributes, not its children, so keep it for that case. When a mismatch appears that you didn't expect, check the console's diff first, then open the page with extensions turned off, in a private window, to rule them out.

examples.title: The date that didn't match
examples.prompt: The line as it was in `src/App.tsx`. The server ran with `TZ=UTC`, which sets its time zone, and a script opened the page in Chromium set to Los Angeles time and printed every error the page reported. The build was made with `NODE_ENV=development`, so React's full messages were included.
examples.explanation: `[pageerror]` is the script's tag for an error the page reported. React names the likely causes, with dates in the visitor's locale among them, then prints the tree down to the text that differed: `+ 9/30/2026` from the browser, `- 10/1/2026` from the server. `<App product=... reviews={Promise}>` at the top is the component, with its props shortened. React regenerated the tree in the browser, so the page still worked and the button still counted. The fix is the line now in `App.tsx`, which adds `{ timeZone: "UTC" }`: both sides then write 10/1/2026, wherever the visitor is.
examples.output:
[pageerror] Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client. As a result this tree will be regenerated on the client. This can happen if a SSR-ed Client Component used: - A server/client branch `if (typeof window !== 'undefined')`. - Variable input such as `Date.now()` or `Math.random()` which changes each time it's called. - Date formatting in a user's locale which doesn't match the server. - External changing data without sending a snapshot of it along with the HTML. - Invalid HTML tag nesting. It can also happen if the client has a browser extension installed which messes with the HTML before React loaded. https://react.dev/link/hydration-mismatch

+ 9/30/2026 - 10/1/2026 ...

steps.title: Prerendering, and caching at a CDN
steps.body:
Rendering for every request costs a server's time on every visit, for pages that are often the same for everyone. Static prerendering makes them once, at build time. And when a page does need a server, a CDN can cache its HTML so most visits never reach it. These are SSG and ISR from the Where HTML Is Made lesson, done by hand.

## Prerendering at build time

`react-dom/static` has `prerender`, which renders like the streaming function but waits for every `Suspense` boundary to finish and returns the whole page at once. That's what you want for a file. `src/entry-prerender.tsx`, the first example, renders one product this way, with its reviews awaited, so they're in the HTML. `prerender.js`, the second example, loops over every product and writes each page to `dist/client/products/<slug>/index.html`.

The result is a folder of plain files. Any static host can serve it, with no Node server at all. The browser shows the full page at once, loads the same client bundle, and hydrates. Since the page carries `__REVIEWS__`, the client needs no API either. Served by Python's small server from the web course, with `python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory dist/client`, the page at `http://localhost:8080/products/storm-shell-jacket/` opens complete and the button counts. The slash at the end matters to Python's server, which redirects the address without it.

The catch is the one from the Where HTML Is Made lesson: the HTML is only as fresh as the last build, and every build makes every page again. So teams prerender what changes rarely, like the home page, guides, and policies, and render the rest per request.

React Router's **framework mode**, a setup of React Router that adds a build step, server rendering, and data loading, has this built in. You list the paths in `react-router.config.ts`:

```ts
import type { Config } from "@react-router/dev/config";

export default {
  ssr: false,
  async prerender() {
    return ["/", "/about", "/products/storm-shell-jacket", "/products/merino-base-layer"];
  },
} satisfies Config;
```

With `ssr: false` and a list of paths, the build writes an HTML file for each, and the rest of the app stays CSR.

## Caching server-rendered pages at a CDN

ISR is a middle path: render on a server, but only now and then. With plain React, you get it from HTTP caching and a **CDN**, the network of servers around the world, from the web course, that keeps copies of your responses close to visitors. Your server sends one header, as `render` does in part 2:

```http
Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300
```

These are the two values from the Where HTML Is Made lesson. `s-maxage=60` lets a **shared cache** like a CDN, but not the visitor's browser, keep this page for 60 seconds. `stale-while-revalidate=300` lets it go on sending that copy for 300 seconds more, while it asks your server for a fresh one in the background. The third example shows the header on a real response.

```diagram server-rendering-cdn
Most visits stop at the CDN. Only a miss, or a stale copy being refreshed, reaches your server.
```

In the diagram, step 1 is a visit while the copy is fresh: the CDN answers without asking your server. In step 2, the copy is between 60 and 360 seconds old: the visitor still gets it at once, and the CDN starts a refresh. In step 3, your server renders a new page, which the next visitor gets. Only after 360 seconds with no visits does a visitor wait for your server.

## Purging on demand

Waiting up to a minute is fine for reviews and wrong for a price that just changed. So CDNs let you purge, as the Where HTML Is Made lesson said: throw away cached copies of chosen URLs at once, through their API or dashboard. Many also let a response carry **cache tags**, like a header naming the product, so a purge by tag clears every page that shows it. Your backend calls the purge when a product changes, and the next visit renders fresh.

That's ISR built from parts: a server that renders, headers, a CDN, and purge calls in the right places. Frameworks like Next.js package all of it, which the Next.js course covers.

examples.title: Rendering one page to a string
examples.explanation: `prerender` takes the same element and the same bootstrap options as `renderToPipeableStream`, and resolves once everything, `Suspense` boundaries included, has rendered. Its `prelude` is a web stream of the finished HTML, and `new Response(prelude).text()` is a short way to read a whole stream into a string. The reviews are awaited here, unlike in `render`, so they're written into the page, and they go into `__REVIEWS__` too, so the browser can hydrate the list without asking an API. A product that doesn't exist throws, which stops the build, since a missing page is a mistake worth seeing.

examples.title: Writing every product page
examples.prompt: `prerender.js` in the project's root, run with `npm run prerender` after `npm run build`.
examples.explanation: It reads the manifest for the bundle's hashed name, the same way the server does, then renders each product and writes the HTML into `dist/client`, next to the assets. `products/storm-shell-jacket/index.html` is the file a static host sends for `/products/storm-shell-jacket/`. Each page took about a second, since `getReviews` waits on purpose, so three pages took three seconds. Pages are independent, so a real build renders many at once, which is what the `concurrency` option in React Router's `prerender` setting does.

examples.title: The header a CDN reads
examples.prompt: With `npm start` running, ask the server for a product page's headers.
examples.explanation: The status line and `Content-Type` are what any page sends. `Cache-Control` is the line a CDN in front of this server would act on: share it, keep it for a minute, and serve it stale for five more while refreshing. Browsers ignore `s-maxage`, so a visitor's own browser asks again next time, which reaches the CDN and is fast. `Connection: keep-alive` means Node keeps the connection open for more requests, as the web course explained. With no CDN in front, as here, every request still reaches the server.

steps.title: Server Components, and choosing a framework
steps.body:
Everything so far renders the same components twice, once on the server and once in the browser, and sends the browser all of their code. React Server Components change that: some components run only on the server, and their code never ships. They're why most new React projects start from a framework.

## Server-only components

A **Server Component** runs only on the server, at build time or per request. It can be `async`, so it can `await` a database query or a file read right in the component, and it can use secrets, since its code never reaches the browser. What it sends to the browser isn't its code but its output: a description of the elements it rendered, which React turns into DOM. It can't use state, effects, or event handlers, since nothing of it runs in the browser.

A **Client Component** is the kind you've written all course, with state and handlers. In a Server Components app, a file that starts with the line `"use client"` marks the boundary: that component and everything it imports are sent to the browser, rendered on the server for the first HTML, and hydrated as in part 3. The first example is a product page as a Server Component, and the second is the Add to cart button inside it, as a Client Component.

The win is in the bundle. The product page's code, its data-fetching code, a Markdown library that formats the description, all of it stays on the server. Only the button's few lines ship. For content-heavy pages that's often most of the JavaScript gone.

## Why it needs a framework

Server Components aren't a function you call like `renderToPipeableStream`. They need three things to agree:

- **The bundler** has to split the code at each `"use client"`, build a server bundle and a browser bundle, and record which client file each boundary needs.
- **The router** has to ask the server for a route's Server Component output on each navigation, and stream it in.
- **The server** has to run the components, serialize their output, and stream it with the HTML.

React provides the pieces, in packages like `react-server-dom-webpack`, but wiring them together is a framework's job. Next.js has done it since 2023, and React Router has been adding it to its framework mode. The Web Vulnerabilities and Secrets lesson's December 2025 advisory was in exactly these packages, which is one more reason to let a framework keep them updated.

## Choosing

| You're building | Start with | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A dashboard or tool behind a login | A Vite SPA, like this course's shop | CSR is enough, hosting is a folder of files, nothing runs on a server |
| A Vite SPA that needs SSR or prerendering for some routes | React Router in framework mode | The same router you know, with server rendering, loaders, and `prerender` added |
| A public site where speed and search matter on every page | Next.js | SSR, SSG, ISR, streaming, and Server Components built in and tuned to work together |

The hand-built server in this lesson isn't what you'd ship. It has no routing beyond one pattern, no caching of data, no error pages, and the reviews are fetched twice. But every framework does what it did: render to a stream, send a bootstrap script, hydrate with the same data, and set cache headers. When a framework's page is slow or a hydration error appears, you now know what's happening underneath. The Next.js course builds on exactly this.

The shop now renders in every way this course covers. The last section, Testing, proves that it works, starting with the next lesson, Unit and Component Tests.

examples.title: A product page as a Server Component
examples.prompt: `app/products/[slug]/page.tsx` in a framework that supports Server Components, like Next.js. The `db` module is the app's own data layer, which only the server can import.
examples.explanation: The component is `async` and awaits a database query directly: no `useEffect`, no API endpoint, no loading state, and no TanStack Query, since the data is fetched where the database is. `params` is a promise that the framework fills from the URL. None of this file's code goes to the browser, not even `formatPrice`, which runs here. The only part that does is `AddToCartButton`, because its file is marked `"use client"`. The framework renders this to HTML for the first visit, and to a compact description of the elements for later navigations.

examples.title: The button as a Client Component
examples.explanation: `"use client"` must be the very first line, before the imports. From here down, this file and what it imports, the cart store and Zustand, are bundled for the browser. The button is still rendered on the server for the first HTML, then hydrated, exactly as in part 3. Props crossing the boundary from a Server Component must be data that can be serialized, like strings, numbers, and plain objects, so `slug` works, but a function prop wouldn't. Keep `"use client"` as low in the tree as you can: everything above it stays on the server.

recap:
- A Vite build is CSR: one empty shell for every address, plus a bundle, served with an SPA fallback rule.
- `renderToPipeableStream` sends the shell at once and streams each `Suspense` boundary when its data is ready.
- The server build exports `render`, the manifest names the client bundle, and `bootstrapModules` loads it.
- `hydrateRoot` attaches handlers to the server's HTML, and needs the same data the server used.
- Dates, randomness, and browser checks cause hydration mismatches: agree on both sides, use effects, or `useId`.
- `prerender` from `react-dom/static` writes complete pages at build time, which any static host can serve.
- `s-maxage` with `stale-while-revalidate` on a CDN, plus purges, gives you ISR by hand.
- Server Components run only on the server and need a framework, so pick a Vite SPA, React Router framework mode, or Next.js by need.
